04 — Executive summary (monthly-report story)¶

Stage 4 of the time-series analytics project. Everything the working notebooks 01-03 found is condensed here into one report: the table of findings, the four dashboard answers (§1 trend, §2 seasonal peak, §3 weekly profile, §4 model choice), and a single verdict for a monthly report.

Status: DESCRIPTIVE / EXPLORATORY. No forecasting, no significance tests; the verdict reports what the data showed.

Inputs: this notebook reuses the three PNG figures built in stages 1-3 (embedded from assets/) and recomputes the headline summary numbers from src/ so every claim below is reproduced by executed code in this notebook.

How to read this notebook¶

  1. Every number in the prose is an executed value. The findings table below (and the per-section cells) computes each headline number from src/ in this notebook; the verdict quotes only printed values. Nothing is typed from memory.
  2. The table of findings is the centerpiece — it is the one screen that carries the whole monthly-report story.
  3. Figures are reused, not re-drawn: three PNGs from stages 1-3 are embedded, one per dashboard question (trend, peak, weekly profile). The model-choice question is answered by the numbers in §4, not by a fourth figure.

comp_net = stl_decompose(daily)
tr = comp_net['trend']
weekly = daily.groupby(daily.index.dayofweek).mean()
seasonal_dow = comp_net['seasonal'].groupby(comp_net.index.dayofweek).mean()
weekday_names = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun']

pos = daily.copy()
for day in zero_days.index:
    pos[day] = (daily.shift(1)[day] + daily.shift(-1)[day]) / 2
cmp = decompose_additive_vs_multiplicative(pos)
add_rrs = cmp['additive']['resid_relative_std']
mult_rrs = cmp['multiplicative']['resid_relative_std']

holidays = national_holidays(HOLIDAYS, daily.index.min().date(),
                            daily.index.max().date())
top = comp_net['resid'].abs().nlargest(15)
hd = holidays.set_index('date')['description']
def holiday_names(d):
    if d not in hd.index:
        return ''
    vals = hd.loc[d]
    vals = [vals] if isinstance(vals, str) else list(vals)
    return ', '.join(vals)
n_holiday = int(sum(holiday_names(d) != '' for d in top.index))

tr_yearly = tr.groupby(tr.index.year).mean()

1. Trend — is there a long-term one, and where does it point?¶

The STL trend (top panel below; raw series in thin gray for context) climbs from 462,484 (first day) to a peak of 1,010,730 in late 2016, then eases to a last value of 745,999 (2017-08-15). The yearly trend means quantify the direction: 385,121 in 2013, 931,604 as the 2016-12 monthly mean, 846,530 in 2017. The trend strength F_t = 0.793 (Wang, Smith & Hyndman 2006) says the trend band absorbs most of the non-seasonal variation — a durable level story, not random wobble. It is not a monotone ramp: it peaks in late 2016 and softens through 2017, so «up then easing» is the honest shape.

The 0-filled Christmas closures are visible as the needle-dips in the top panel; they belong to the residual story (section 2), not to the trend.

2. Seasonal peak — when, and why (national holidays)¶

Two different «peaks» answer this from the STL decomposition:

  • The regular weekly peak is Sunday. With period=7 the seasonal band cycles every week; mean seasonal by weekday peaks on Sunday (+215,863 units) and bottoms on Thursday (−136,391) — the same weekday shape Stage 1 measured on raw means (Sun ≈ 822k vs Thu ≈ 503k, printed in cell 4), now isolated from noise.
  • The calendar peaks are national-holiday events. The weekly band cannot encode a specific date, so single-day events land in the residual: 14 of the top-15 largest |resid| days are exactly a national-holiday date (table in the cell below). The biggest are the four Navidad (Christmas) closures — 2016-12-25 reaches −1,321,021 — and the New Year bursts (+1,262,485 on 2017-01-01). One top-15 day has no named holiday: 2017-04-01, the largest raw-sales day of the whole series (1,463,084, printed in the setup cell) — the holiday file does not explain it.

So: expect a Sunday-heavy week every week, and the outlier days around Christmas / New Year as the seasonal peaks for calendar dates.

3. Weekly profile — where the weekday rhythm lives¶

The bar figure (reused from Stage 1) is the network-wide mean by day of week: Sun ≈ 821,794 and Sat ≈ 772,206 against a Thursday trough of ≈ 503,173 — an amplitude of 318,621 units (exact numbers in the findings table, row 4). This is the pattern the period=7 STL seasonal band captures and isolates, and it is why smoothing with a 7-day window (stage 2) removes the noise while keeping the level.

4. Model choice — additive or multiplicative?¶

decompose_additive_vs_multiplicative fits an additive STL on the original scale and a multiplicative proxy (STL on log, components exp-mapped back) on the identical, strictly-positive input. The four 0-filled closure days are replaced by neighbour means only here, and the adjusted rows are printed (cell 12) so the policy is auditable.

Decision rule (documented in src/decomposition.py): pick the model with the smaller resid_relative_std. Result on the network series: additive 0.1323 vs multiplicative 0.1311 — the multiplicative proxy wins by 0.94% of relative residual spread. That margin is tiny, no test was run on the gap, and both fits tell the same monthly-report story; we record multiplicative as the pick and report the near-tie rather than overselling it.

In [6]:
zero_days = daily[daily == 0]
adj = []
for day in zero_days.index:
    left, right = daily.shift(1)[day], daily.shift(-1)[day]
    adj.append((day.date(), float(daily[day]), float(left),
                float(right), float(pos[day])))
print('adjusted closure days (original -> neighbour mean):')
print(pd.DataFrame(adj, columns=['date', 'original', 'prev', 'next',
                                'replacement']).to_string(index=False))
rows = []
for model in ('additive', 'multiplicative'):
    e = cmp[model]
    rows.append({
        'model': model,
        'resid_relative_std': e['resid_relative_std'],
        'resid std': float(e['resid'].std()),
    })
with pd.option_context('display.float_format', lambda v: f'{v:.4f}'):
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
print(f'recommendation: {cmp["recommendation"]} (documented rule: '
      'smaller resid_relative_std wins)')
print(f'gap (mult - add)/add: {(mult_rrs - add_rrs) / add_rrs:+.2%}')

5. Verdict — the answer for a monthly report¶

This is the executive answer to the question a monthly report asks: what happened to daily network sales, descriptively?

The network grew strongly from 2013 through late 2016 (STL trend strength F_t = 0.793; yearly trend means 385,121 → 846,530) and then eased into 2017. Sales follow a stable weekly rhythm that peaks on Sunday (mean +215,863 seasonal units above the weekday midpoint; trough Thursday at −136,391), and the calendar outliers are national holidays: 14 of the 15 largest residual days fall exactly on a holiday, led by the Christmas-network closures (Navidad 2016 at −1,321,021) and New Year bursts (+1,262,485 on 2017-01-01). Between the additive and multiplicative seasonal models the data pick multiplicative, but only by 0.94% of relative residual spread — the two are effectively tied for reporting purposes.

Honest boundary of this verdict: it is descriptive and exploratory (status of all stages 1-4). It describes what the STL decomposition showed; it does not forecast, fit an ARIMA family model, or claim statistical significance for any single number. The trend's late-2016 easing and the one unexplained top-residual day (2017-04-01) are facts we state without a causal story. For a decision that forecasts — e.g. «will 2017 keep growing» — a separate, pre-registered modeling stage would be needed; this report's job is only to say what the series has done.
